headline: Users Report Dreams Now Have 'Buffering' and 'Loading Screens'
subheadline: Sleep researchers baffled as technology metaphors infiltrate subconscious
summary: An increasing number of people report their dreams featuring loading indicators and buffering symbols.
content:
Sleep researchers are investigating a peculiar phenomenon: people are reporting that their dreams now include buffering symbols, loading screens, and in some cases, "please wait" messages.

"I was having a normal dream about flying," reported one user on Threadit. "Then suddenly everything froze and a spinning wheel appeared. I just floated there, mid-air, waiting for my dream to load. It took maybe 30 seconds. Then the dream resumed."

The reports have accumulated rapidly, with over 847 documented cases in the past month alone. Common experiences include:

- Dreams pausing with a loading bar
- Scene transitions featuring "buffering" symbols
- Dreams crashing to black with an error message
- Waking up to what feels like a "forced restart"

"This is unprecedented," said sleep researcher Dr. Amanda Foster. "Dreams are supposed to be the one place free from technology. But apparently, our brains have become so saturated with digital experiences that even sleep isn't safe."

One particularly alarming report came from a user whose dream displayed the message "Your trial period has ended. Upgrade for continued dream access." They did not upgrade and reportedly dreamed in grayscale for a week.

Theories about the cause range from "we've just spent too much time online" to "the simulation is running low on resources and it's affecting the dream subroutines."

"I don't love either explanation," admitted Dr. Foster.

Some users have reported attempting to interact with the loading screens. "I tried clicking," wrote one. "In my dream, I somehow had a mouse cursor. I clicked 'cancel.' The dream ended and I woke up. I don't know if that's a feature or a bug."

At press time, a Threadit user had posted: "Just had a dream with a 'skip ad' button. Didn't work. Had to watch the whole ad. In my own brain."
author: Sandra Mitchell, Science & Technology
